section.title: Why multivariable calculus begins with geometry
section.p: Single-variable calculus lived on a line. A point was described by one number, and there were only two directions to move: left or right. But many real-life questions do not live on a real line. A storm moves across a map, a satellite moves through space, and the temperature in a room depends on where you stand.

subsection.title: From one input to many inputs
subsection.p: Imagine a small weather station on the coast. A radar image says that the center of a storm cell is 12 \text{ km east}, \qquad 5 \text{ km north} of the station. The location is naturally written as the ordered pair P=(12,5). A helicopter hovering above the same point needs a third number. If it is 0.8 km above the ground, its position is H=(12,5,0.8).

The numbers in these lists do not all have the same meaning. The first two numbers locate a point on a flat map. The third number locates height. But the idea is the same: a position is described by several coordinates.

figure.caption: The storm moves from P to Q, requiring a larger coordinate grid.

subsection.p: This is the first reason multivariable calculus begins with geometry. Before we can differentiate or integrate, we need to know where things are.

subsection.title: Position, displacement, and measured quantities
subsection.p: Now suppose the storm moves. One hour later its center is Q=(15,9). We can subtract the coordinates to find the displacement: Q-P=(15-12,\;9-5)=(3,4). That means the storm moved 3 km east and 4 km north.
If it moved in a straight line, the distance traveled is found from the same Pythagorean theorem used in the plane: \sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5 \text{ km}.

statement.p: The point P=(12,5) is a location. The ordered pair (3,4) is a displacement. It tells us how to move from P to Q: (12,5)+(3,4)=(15,9). The same displacement could start somewhere else: (2,1)+(3,4)=(5,5). So a displacement is not tied to one fixed place. It can be applied to any point.

subsection.p: This distinction is small, but it will save us from confusion later.
A point is a location. A vector is a displacement. Coordinates let us write both with ordered lists, but the meanings are different.

statement.p: One drone lifts off from the rooftop R=(2,1); a second drone lifts off from a different rooftop S=(7,3). Both receive the same instruction, the displacement (4,4). Without computing either landing point, decide two things and say why: do the drones end at the same place, and does the pair (4,4) on its own tell you where either drone is? In one sentence, what does a displacement record, and what does it deliberately leave out?

hint.p: Ask what question each ordered pair answers. A point answers where?; a displacement answers which way, and how far? Try applying the same instruction at two different starting points and notice whether the change depends on where you began.

subsection.title: A first story: locating a storm, a satellite, and a temperature reading
subsection.p: The same coordinates can also be used as inputs to a function.

At the point (12,5), a weather sensor might report a temperature of 18^\circC. Then temperature is not itself a point. It is a number assigned to a point: T(12,5)=18. If the temperature is measured over a whole region, we have a function T(x,y). The input is a point on a map, and the output is a number.
A satellite position is different. At time t, the satellite has three coordinates: \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)). Here the input is one number, time, but the output is a point in space.
So several kinds of functions will appear in this book:

table.title: Kinds of functions appearing in this book.

subsection.p: The last example is especially important. A wind field assigns an arrow to every point. At one point the wind may blow east; at another, northeast; at another, not at all. Later, this idea will become a vector field. Vector fields are the natural language of fluids, force, electricity, magnetism, and many of the integral theorems near the end of the book.

statement.p: On the same weather map, the temperature reading T(x,y) and the wind \mathbf F(x,y) are both functions of position. Yet only one of them is called a vector field. Without writing any formulas, explain what the wind output carries at each point that the temperature output does not, and why that difference is exactly what earns the wind the name vector field.

hint.p: Picture standing at one spot and asking, What does this map hand me here? The thermometer hands you a single number; the wind hands you something you could draw as an arrow. Think about what an arrow records that a number alone cannot.

subsection.title: What changes from single-variable calculus, and what stays the same
subsection.p: Single-variable calculus asked questions like these: \text{How fast is } f(x) \text{ changing?} and \text{How much has accumulated from } a \text{ to } b?
Those questions remain. But the geometry changes.

For a function of one variable, the graph is a curve in the plane. At a point, there is one main direction to move along the input line. For a function of two variables, the graph is usually a surface in space. At a point in the input plane, there are infinitely many directions to move.
A hiker standing on a hillside can walk north, south, east, west, or along any slanted path between them. A single slope number no longer tells the whole story.

exercise.title: Why one slope is not enough?

statement.p: On a single-variable graph, asking how steep is it here? has one answer. On a hillside, the same question feels incomplete until you add something. What is the missing piece of information that the hiker must supply before how steep? becomes a sensible question, and why did that piece never come up on the number line?

hint.p: On a line there were only two ways to move, so the answer was forced. On a hill the hiker gets to choose a way to step. Think about what changes between facing uphill and facing along the slope at the same spot.

subsection.p: The last line is the beginning of the long story of the book. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus will not disappear. It will generalize.

For now, the next step is much simpler. The difference between two locations behaves like a reusable instruction: \text{move } 3 \text{ east and } 4 \text{ north}. That instruction is the first object we need to understand carefully. It is called a vector.
